Title: Does positive attribute framing work better in promoting AI-powered services? Boundary conditions of the valence-consistent shift effect
Authors: Wu Y.; Lin C.; Xie C.; Yang C.
Abstract: The Valence-Consistent Shift (VCS) effect–a foundational principle in framing theory–holds that consumers generally respond more favorably to positively framed information than to negatively framed information. While this effect is well established in human-delivered service contexts, its applicability to AI-powered service encounters remains underexplored. This study investigates whether, and under what conditions, the VCS effect works in AI-powered services. Five studies demonstrate that positive attribute framing generally works better than negative attribute framing in promoting AI-powered services. However, this effect reverses when the service is personalized (vs. standardized) and may attenuate when the decision-maker is the service provider (vs. service receiver). Drawing on regulatory focus theory and processing fluency, we further identify the underlying psychological mechanism driving these effects. This research extends the VCS effect to AI-powered service contexts by identifying boundary conditions under which the effect is strengthened, weakened, or reversed. It also provides evidence that processing fluency helps explain how attribute framing interacts with AI-powered service contexts to influence customer response. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
Keywords: AI service marketing; AI-powered services; Attribute framing; Processing fluency; Service provider and service receiver; Valence-consistent shift effect
Journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
evidence: positive attribute framing generally works better than negative attribute framing in promoting AI-powered services
rationale: The study tests how attribute framing in AI-powered service encounters influences customer responses, i.e., a marketing promotion/communication decision. The mechanism centers on psychological processing (e.g., processing fluency) and customer response, aligning with Feeling AI rather than automation/prediction objectives (R1, R3).

Title: When humor beats believability: How AI-generated imagery shapes pet-inclusive restaurant choice
Authors: Chan J.
Abstract: This study delineates how stylized AI‑generated and naturalistic traditional imagery shape pet owners’ responses in pet‑inclusive restaurant marketing through distinct cognitive and affective processes. Grounded in the Cognitive Appraisal Framework, two experiments examine context-specific appraisal mechanisms. Drawing on Mind Perception Theory, Study 1 shows that naturalistic traditional pet-only images enhance believability, which in turn strengthens mind attribution (agency and experience) and, subsequently, behavioral intentions. Study 2, applying Benign Violation Theory to pet–owner dyads, reveals a practical trade‑off: although AI‑generated images reduce perceived quality, they elicit stronger perceived humor, and this humor‑driven affective route increases visit intention and willingness to pay. Overall, the findings indicate two context-specific appraisal patterns: traditional pet-only imagery supports credibility-oriented responses, whereas AI-generated dyadic imagery supports humor-driven engagement. These results reflect distinct visual conditions rather than direct comparisons of image types alone. Practical implications are provided for selecting visual formats to improve pet-inclusive restaurant marketing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
Keywords: AI-generated imagery; Believability; Benign violation theory; Perceived humor; Pet owner decision-making

rationale: The AI-generated imagery is used as a marketing communication format to shape restaurant choice intentions and willingness to pay. Because the effects operate through perceived humor and affective routes, the AI’s purpose aligns with Feeling AI (R2).

Title: Whimsical threat? The impact of virtual influencers’ cuteness on compensatory consumption
Authors: Li S.; Zhou M.; Huang Y.; Zhang H.
Abstract: Cuteness is a sharing strategy in virtual influencer (VI) marketing, yet little is known about how VI's cuteness types influence consumer decision making. This research investigates how distinct VI cuteness types (kindchenschema vs. whimsical) influence consumers' compensatory consumption intentions. Based on self congruity theory and compensatory consumer behavior model, this research ascertains the mechanism of how VI cuteness types influence compensatory consumption across five experiments (N = 1862). Findings indicate that whimsically (vs. kindchenschema) cute VIs increase consumers' preference for compensatory products by evoking more identity threats in consumers. This effect is further disappeared when VIs have low artificial intelligence capability, or when consumers have high self-concept clarity. These insights contribute to the literature of virtual influencer marketing and compensatory consumption, offering imperative managerial guidance for marketers on leveraging VIs for effective marketing strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
Keywords: Artificial intelligence capability; Compensatory consumption; Cuteness; Identity threat; Self-concept clarity; Virtual influencer
Journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
evidence: whimsically (vs. kindchenschema) cute VIs increase consumers' preference for compensatory products by evoking more identity threats in consumers
rationale: Virtual influencer (VI) “cuteness” content is used in marketing to persuade consumers toward compensatory product preferences. The causal mechanism is identity threat (an affective/identity-oriented response), so the AI’s purpose fits Feeling AI (R1, R2).

Title: How should conversational recommendation agents organize candidate products? Matching recommendation set granularity with time pressure
Authors: Wang Q.; Tong W.; Wei T.Y.; Fan X.Q.; Zhang W.
Abstract: With the widespread application of conversational recommendation agents (CRA) on e-commerce platforms, an increasing number of consumers use a CRA to support product choices. Existing research has mainly focused on the accuracy of CRA recommendations, with limited attention paid to how candidate products should be organized and whether this organization should be adapted to consumers' current decision contexts. Drawing on the product set granularity perspective and the heuristic–systematic model, this study examines the matching effect between recommendation set granularity (coarse vs. fine) and time pressure (high vs. low) on consumers' intention to adopt CRA recommendations and investigates the underlying psychological mechanisms. The results of three online scenario experiments reveal that consumers show higher adoption intention toward CRA recommendations featuring coarse recommendation set granularity under high time pressure and toward those featuring fine recommendation set granularity under low time pressure. The two matching effects operate through perceived fluency and perceived attractiveness, respectively. Furthermore, consumer knowledge affects the relative effectiveness of the two matching strategies: the match between coarse recommendation set granularity and high time pressure is more effective for consumers with low product knowledge, whereas the match between fine recommendation set granularity and low time pressure is more effective for consumers with high product knowledge. These findings extend CRA research from recommendation content to the organization of candidate products and provide guidance for retail platforms to adjust recommendation set granularity according to consumers’ time pressure and product knowledge. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
Keywords: Conversational recommendation; Heuristic–systematic model; Perceived attractiveness; Perceived fluency; Recommendation set granularity; Time pressure
Journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
evidence: The results of three online scenario experiments reveal that consumers show higher adoption intention toward CRA recommendations featuring coarse recommendation set granularity under high time pressure and toward those featuring fine recommendation set granularity under low time pressure.
rationale: Conversational recommendation agents organize candidate products to increase adoption intention, supporting a recommendation-based marketing action for product choice. The decision is recommendation support (a thinking/personalized decision purpose), not automation of routine tasks (R3).

Title: Chatbot service quality in omnichannel retailing: Effects of ChatbotSQ on decision confidence and customer behavior
Authors: Abbas F.A.; Carlson J.; Rahman S.M.; Gudergan S.P.
Abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly being embedded in omnichannel retail ecosystems; however, research on how chatbot service quality relates to customer behavior is limited. In this paper, we conceptualize chatbot service quality (ChatbotSQ) as a formative construct comprising six dimensions: functional, integration, interface, safety, emotional, and personalization quality. Drawing on means-end chain theory, we examine decision confidence as a mechanism underlying the association between chatbot service quality and customers' share of time with the chatbot and omnichannel ecosystem lock-in and explore the moderating role of chatbot comfort level. We use partial least squares structural equation modeling, importance-performance map analysis, and necessary condition analysis to analyze survey data from the United States (N = 345) and Saudi Arabia (N = 302). The results show that chatbot service quality is positively associated with customers' share of time with the chatbot and omnichannel ecosystem lock-in in both countries. These relationships are mediated by decision confidence, which also emerged as a necessary condition for achieving both behavioral outcomes. Chatbot comfort level significantly moderates the relationship between ChatbotSQ and decision confidence in Saudi Arabia but not in the United States, indicating that this boundary condition is context-sensitive across the two samples examined. We also validate a condensed six-item ChatbotSQ measure that provides a parsimonious alternative for research and practice. These findings advance retailing research by showing that AI chatbot service quality is associated with behavioral outcomes through customers’ decision confidence. © 2026 The Authors
Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Chatbots; Customer experience; Marketing strategies; Necessary condition analysis; Omnichannel retail; PLS-SEM
Journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
evidence: we conceptualize chatbot service quality (ChatbotSQ) as a formative construct comprising six dimensions: functional, integration, interface, safety, emotional, and personalization quality.
rationale: The study evaluates an AI chatbot embedded in omnichannel retail, linking its service quality to customers’ decision confidence and behavior—an AI deployment in a frontline service interaction. Because it explicitly includes emotional and personalization quality and examines confidence as a customer experience mechanism, it fits Feeling AI (R5, R2).

Title: Development of optimization mechanism for cross-border e-commerce logistics using genetic algorithm: scenario of home appliance from Japan to East China
Authors: Huang Y.; Shen L.; Xu L.; Yan H.
Abstract: To address the challenges of high costs, volatility, and multiple constraints in cross-border e-commerce logistics of home appliances from Japan to East China, this study proposes a two-segment chromosome genetic algorithm (GA) optimization mechanism to systematically compare ten logistics operation models that are currently feasible for enterprises. The first segment encodes the suitability of candidate logistics models, while the second segment simultaneously evolves the weight coefficient of key performance indicators. A global search is conducted in a multi-objective space using fitness-proportional selection, BLX-α crossover, and adaptive Gaussian mutation through which both the suitability and the coefficient weights are synchronously adjusted during the search process to obtain a comprehensive evaluation that is more consistent with real business scenarios. The experiment is based on company-collected operational data and industry survey results, incorporating transportation, warehousing, return logistics, and carbon emissions. The GA results indicate that the Off-peak Transit Time is the most critical performance indicator, leading to a strong preference for air shipping, with approximately 60% of orders allocated to air consolidation. As reason, the time and inventory costs associated with short-sea routes weaken the traditional advantages of sea shipping, while the economies of scale of consolidation offset the typically high cost of air shipping. The study demonstrates the applicability of an enhanced GA in medium-range cross-border logistics system design, offering practical decision support for enterprises seeking a balanced trade-off among cost efficiency, lead time, service quality, and sustainability. © The Author(s) 2026.
Keywords: Cross-border e-commerce; Genetic algorithm; Japan–China marketing; Logistics operations; Multi-objective optimization

rationale: The AI is used to optimize cross-border logistics operations (transportation/warehousing/returns), which is a place/convenience (logistics/delivery) marketing action. A genetic algorithm is used to generate improved decisions via optimization/learning from business data, aligning with Thinking AI (R3).

Title: From Information Asymmetry to Sustainable Demand Release: How Human–Machine Trust Shapes AI Agent-Enabled Rural Cultural Tourism Intention
Authors: Wang Y.; Li J.; Peng X.; Peng L.; Liu X.
Abstract: Sustainable rural cultural tourism requires effective approaches to improving the visibility, accessibility, and decision feasibility of dispersed cultural resources, particularly in destinations where service information is fragmented across online and offline channels and tourists face substantial uncertainty in coordinating transport, accommodation, and cultural experiences. This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) agents can support the sustainable digital transformation of rural cultural tourism by alleviating information asymmetry, releasing latent tourism demand, and facilitating calibrated human–machine trust. Drawing on human–machine trust theory and the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this study conceptualizes AI agent functionality through three dimensions: AI Information Quality (AIQ), Information Extensibility (IE), and AI Planning Autonomy (APA). Travel Planning Risk Awareness (TPRA), Human–Machine Trust (HMT), Planning Satisfaction (PS), Rural Cultural Tourism Attractiveness (RCTA), and Rural Cultural Tourism Intention (RCTI) are further incorporated into an integrated model comprising four pathways: information empowerment, autonomy–risk awareness tension, trust boundary, and demand release. Using the Ctrip AI Travel Assistant as the research context, 413 valid questionnaire responses were analyzed through a hybrid Structural Equation Modeling–Artificial Neural Network approach. The results support 12 of the 14 hypotheses. AIQ significantly influences IE (β = 0.530), PS (β = 0.304), and HMT (β = 0.380). HMT functions as a central mechanism connecting AI empowerment with tourism decision-making and exerts the strongest effect on RCTA (β = 0.485), reaching 100% normalized importance in the corresponding ANN model. TPRA positively affects HMT (β = 0.262), indicating that risk awareness can facilitate rational and calibrated trust rather than simply inhibiting AI acceptance. RCTA (β = 0.281) and PS (β = 0.218) jointly promote RCTI through the complementary mechanisms of destination pull and planning push. The findings demonstrate that AI agents can contribute to the sustainable development of rural cultural tourism by improving information accessibility, strengthening responsible human–AI collaboration, and transforming fragmented cultural resources into credible and actionable travel-planning options. This study provides implications for sustainable destination marketing, responsible AI travel-service design, rural revitalization, and the long-term development of rural cultural tourism, while clarifying trust as a psychological gate in AI empowerment. © 2026 by the authors.
Keywords: AI agents; demand release; human–machine trust; information asymmetry; rural cultural tourism intention; SEM-ANN; sustainable rural tourism
evidence: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) agents can support the sustainable digital transformation of rural cultural tourism by alleviating information asymmetry, releasing latent tourism demand, and facilitating calibrated human–machine trust.
rationale: The study models how an AI travel assistant affects tourists’ trust and intention, supporting understanding of how AI influences tourism decision-making. The psychological mechanisms (trust/gates/risk awareness) align with Feeling AI (R5).

Title: User experiences in fishing tourism
Authors: Sánchez F.T.; Martin-Fuentes E.; Verdicia V.P.
Abstract: This study aims to address the limited academic exploration of fishing tourism by means of Pine and Gilmore’s established experiential marketing model by analysing online reviews of fishing tourism activities on TripAdvisor. To do so, we use machine learning techniques combining supervised and unsupervised analysis and with graphic value, which favours decision-making for tourism operators. Our results highlight a clear emphasis on user satisfaction in the overall model, with a significant connection to the escapist sense of the experience. Unsupervised association analysis suggests that user enjoyment across experiential components positively influences satisfaction. It also allows to visualise the Fishing Tourism user's behaviour according to two types of activity: Charter Fishing Tourism, with an active presence of the escapist component, and Combined Fishing Tourism, characterised by a more passive integration–entertainment and aesthetic–of the user in the activity. The study concludes that improvements in one experiential realm can impact others. Methodologically, the use of AI for sentence-level analysis enhances the understanding of relationships between expressions and variables. The expanded model, incorporating new variables like tourism satisfaction and loyalty, reflects the complexity of the contemporary tourism industry. © 2025 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.
Keywords: Fishing tourism; machine learning; netnography; user experience; user-generated content

Title: A Hybrid NSGA-II and Machine Learning Framework for Multi-Objective Marketing Budget Optimization in Kazakhstan’s Agro-Industrial Complex
Authors: Kalpeyeva Z.; Abildaeva Z.; Uskenbayeva R.; Kassymova A.; Kutlimuratov A.; Allayarov P.; Abdusalomov A.; Cho Y.-I.
Abstract: The agro-industrial complex of Kazakhstan faces increasing pressure to improve the efficiency of marketing activities under conditions of limited budgets, regional heterogeneity, seasonal demand, and uneven digital infrastructure. Traditional marketing planning methods often rely on expert judgment or single-objective optimization and therefore cannot adequately address the conflicting objectives of maximizing marketing effectiveness, expanding audience coverage, and minimizing campaign expenditure. This study proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that combines the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) with machine learning-based clustering for multi-objective marketing budget optimization in the agro-industrial sector. The model considers five major promotion channels: digital media, television, radio, print media, and events. NSGA-II is used to generate Pareto-optimal budget allocation strategies, while K-means clustering classifies the resulting solutions into interpretable strategy groups. The framework was evaluated using synthetic data and enterprise-level data reflecting marketing conditions in Kazakhstan. Results show that strategies combining digital media and television achieve the highest marketing effectiveness and audience coverage, although they require greater campaign expenditure. Radio and print media remain relevant for cost-sensitive strategies, particularly for enterprises with limited resources. Cluster analysis identified three main strategy groups: cost-efficient, balanced, and high-performance configurations. The findings confirm that marketing budget allocation in the agro-industrial sector should be treated as a multi-objective optimization problem rather than a single-criterion decision. The proposed framework provides both computational optimization and managerial interpretability, supporting data-driven, adaptive, and resource-aware marketing planning for agro-industrial enterprises in Kazakhstan. © 2026 by the authors.
Keywords: K-means clustering; machine learning; marketing budget optimization; multi-objective optimization; Pareto optimization
evidence: NSGA-II is used to generate Pareto-optimal budget allocation strategies, while K-means clustering classifies the resulting solutions into interpretable strategy groups.
rationale: The AI is explicitly used for multi-objective marketing budget optimization across promotion channels, supporting a promotion/communication action decision. Since NSGA-II generates optimized budget strategies (new decision/policy recommendations), the intelligence is Thinking AI (R3).

Title: Authenticity in the Age of Generative AI: Reimagining Host-Guest Relations in Travel Planning
Authors: Yang L.; Leung X.Y.; Xiong W.
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is transforming how travelers plan trips, yet research has not fully examined dynamic interactions between travelers and generative AI or the co-creation of authenticity through these interactions. This exploratory qualitative study employs a retrospective think-aloud method to explore how travelers engage with generative AI. Grounded in the lenses of host-guest relations and authenticity, this study conceptualizes travel planning as a co-performance between the digital guest (the traveler) and the digital host (generative AI). Findings identify six AI roles (mentor, pathfinder, partner, acquaintance, butler, and implementer) shaped by power dynamics and encounter depth, and four authenticity pathways (co-creation, co-recovery, co-reduction, and co-destruction) across five pre-travel experience stages: triggering inspiration, shaping vision, gathering details, evaluating information, and making decisions. The study advances a relational and performative framework for understanding human-AI collaboration in tourism and offers practical insights for enhancing AI-assisted destination marketing and traveler experiences. © The Author(s) 2026
Keywords: authenticity; co-creation; generative AI; host-guest relations; human-AI interaction; travel planning

rationale: The study focuses on human–AI interactions during travel planning and how generative AI roles shape co-creation of authenticity, which is primarily knowledge-building about customer experiences/decision processes. Because it concerns interaction roles and co-performance, it aligns with Feeling AI (R2).

Title: Strategic role of artificial intelligence in affecting sustainable performance through moderating effect of performance management of digital marketing activities
Authors: Aljumah A.I.; Nuseir M.T.; ElRefae G.; Hanaysha J.R.; Al Ghuzzi G.A.M.; Alshawabkeh M.
Abstract: The objective of this research was to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) focused digital business strategy helps small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to achieve success in manufacturing by measuring the financial benefits of having a digitally enabled performance measurement in marketing. The study focused on defining a company’s digital business strategy through three parameters: development, objective and resource in United Arab Emirates (UAE). A quantitative methodology was employed, drawing data from 212 managers and key decision-makers in manufacturing firms, and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings of the study found that all three parameters of the AI focused digital business strategy influenced the financial success of manufacturing companies; the biggest influences were from the development and resource parameters. The study also found that performance management in marketing positively impacted the sustainable financial performance of manufacturing companies by directly impacting performance and enhancing the effectiveness of the development and resource parameters. Performance management was found to not have a moderating effect on the objective parameter. These results carry significant implications for practical management solutions, i.e. the need for manufacturing companies to develop a simple strategic plan, align resources, and monitor performance in real-time to better position themselves to achieve long term sustainable financial performance. Furthermore, this study contributes to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 12 by illustrating how AI-driven digital strategies, together with the performance evaluation of digital marketing activities, facilitate more efficient resource utilization and enhance the quality of managerial decision-making. © The Author(s) 2026.
Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Digital business strategy; Digitally marketing; Financial performance; Performance measurement; Sustainability; Sustainable development goals

Title: ICAIMT — Marketers’ Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence Adoption: A Behavioural Reasoning Theory Approach in Egypt — A Thematic Analysis
Authors: Essam R.
Abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) tools across all stages of marketing, from data collection and segmentation to customer engagement and campaign execution, there is limited research on how marketers rationalise AI adoption, particularly in emerging markets such as Egypt. Using Behavioural Reasoning Theory (BRT) as a guiding framework, this study explores Egyptian marketers’ cognitive and value-based perceptions regarding AI tools, including their motivations, concerns, and adoption intentions. Twenty-five in-depth interviews with marketers from diverse sectors were conducted and analysed using thematic analysis, leading to the identification of six major themes: AI tools and uses, values towards AI adoption, reasons for AI adoption, reasons against AI adoption, attitudes towards AI, and adoption intention. Findings show that while marketers generally perceive AI as enhancing marketing effectiveness, concerns persist about job displacement, the erosion of human connection, ethical risks, and technological complexity. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of AI’s role in shaping modern marketing practices within emerging economies. This study extends BRT into the context of AI marketing, highlighting how personal values and contextual factors in emerging markets shape adoption decisions. This research offers practical insights for AI developers, marketing managers, and policymakers aiming to foster more ethical and user-centred AI integration in marketing strategies. © World Scientific Publishing Co.
Keywords: AI adoption; Artificial intelligence; behavioural reasoning theory; emerging markets; marketing; qualitative research; thematic analysis
Journal: Journal of Information and Knowledge Management

Title: MWIN (Measure What Is Needed): a strategic framework for privacy-first, AI-ready, and data-driven marketing analytics
Authors: Gorostiza-Esquerdeiro I.; Buján-Carballal D.; Oyarbide-Zubillaga A.
Abstract: Organizations face the dual challenge of measuring data-driven marketing while adhering to stringent privacy standards and preparing for artificial intelligence. This research introduces MWIN (Measure What Is Needed), a strategic framework that aligns business objectives with KPI definitions and embeds privacy-by-design at the definition layer. Developed through a hybrid Action Research and Design Science program, the framework was evaluated using expert reviews and quantitative indicators against hypotheses covering strategic alignment, privacy compliance, AI-readiness, data quality, and decision-making. Findings indicate that MWIN strengthens KPI traceability, integrates consent controls without eroding analytical utility, and supports higher semantic maturity, better data quality, and more routine evidence-based decisions. The study contributes a mixed-methods template for evaluating socio-technical frameworks and offers practitioners a reproducible path to minimize risk and ready data for advanced analytics. Future research should extend to longitudinal testing and AI fairness profiling to ensure ethical activation at scale. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2026.

Title: Artificial intelligence integration as strategic organisational adaptation: faculty evidence from universities in Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom
Authors: Almoraish A.; Alhakimi W.; Abdullah A.; Al-Mamary Y.H.
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping service practice and increasing pressure on universities to align professional education with emerging technological capabilities. Yet limited research explains how faculty convert changes in AI-enabled services into curriculum integration. This study examines AI integration in services marketing education in Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom. Drawing selectively on the Technology Acceptance Model, the framework incorporates consumer expectations of AI-driven services, faculty attitudes, institutional readiness, perceived usefulness, curriculum relevance perception, AI literacy and cultural orientation. Data from 231 faculties were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. All seven constructs had significant direct effects on AI integration. However, the proposed indirect effects through perceived usefulness and curriculum relevance perception were unsupported. AI literacy negatively moderated the relationship between curriculum relevance perception and integration, while the remaining interaction effects were not significant. Most path differences were nonsignificant, with differences detected for three relationships. The study positions AI integration as an organisationally situated curriculum decision in which perceived usefulness operates alongside professional and organisational influences. It distinguishes organisational feasibility, pedagogical utility and disciplinary legitimacy, while conceptualising AI literacy as both implementation capability and evaluative filter. The findings inform curriculum review, faculty development and procedural support. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.

Title: Enhance ecological validity of scenario-based experiments on human–AI collaboration: evidence from an interactive LLM-based research tool
Authors: Leszczyński G.; Gaczek P.; Mouakher A.
Abstract: Purpose – This paper questions whether traditional experiments accurately reflect decision-making collaborations with AI and addresses this challenge, proposing a novel approach to conducting scenario-based experiments in human–AI collaboration. Design/methodology/approach – This paper presents the managerial interaction and response to artificial intelligence, a tool for researching managers' interactions with AI, addressing the shortcomings of traditional vignette approaches. It utilizes advanced LLMs combined with a reasoning-and-action framework to improve contextual accuracy, interactivity and ecological validity. It also tests the tool's internal validity by applying precision, recall and F1 metrics and ecological validity, comparing it to vignettes tested by 222 mid-level marketing managers. Findings – Evaluation results show that the tool enables participants to engage naturally with AI by integrating experimental variables within a controlled yet dynamic chatbot setting, maintaining both experimental precision and realism. Originality/value – This tool marks a promising advance in AI-manager collaboration research, supporting longitudinal research and cross-cultural validation. © 2026, Emerald Publishing Limited
Keywords: AI; Decision-making; Experiment; Interactions; Validity; Vignette
Journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing

Title: ChatGPT as a Digital Dining Companion: Examining AI Perceptions and Consumer Loyalty in Restaurant Recommendations
Authors: Kim M.; Lee S.-M.
Abstract: Growing artificial intelligence (AI) use in hospitality reshapes consumer decision-making, particularly through AI-driven recommendation systems like ChatGPT. Previous research has largely emphasized the functional aspects of AI recommendations; therefore, this study investigates the psychological and emotional mechanisms that drive consumer loyalty toward ChatGPT for restaurant recommendations. Grounded in the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this study examines perceived warmth, communication speed, and perceived competence as key stimuli influencing consumer experiences. Trust, attitudes toward ChatGPT, parasocial interaction, and psychological ownership mediate consumer loyalty. To ensure a qualified sample, data were collected from 528 participants through a marketing research firm. The findings highlight the significance of both cognitive and emotional dimensions in AI-human interactions, demonstrating that trust and psychological engagement enhance consumer loyalty to AI-driven recommendations. This study advances AI perception frameworks and provides practical insights for marketers and AI developers seeking to optimize AI-driven recommendation systems to foster deeper consumer relationships. © 2026 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.
Keywords: AI-driven recommendation systems; ChatGPT; consumer loyalty; parasocial interaction; psychological ownership

Title: Mapping the intellectual structure of artificial intelligence-enabled customer engagement: a bibliometric analysis and framework-based review for future research directions
Authors: Tagra P.; Rani S.
Abstract: Purpose – Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing by enabling personalization, automation and interactive experiences. The research on AI-enabled customer engagement (AI–CE) remains fragmented, lacking systematic mapping and an integrated framework. This study aims to examine publication trends, contributors and collaborations; map intellectual and knowledge structures; and develop a framework identifying enablers, challenges and future research opportunities. Design/methodology/approach – This study followed a two-stage design combining bibliometric and thematic analysis. Data were retrieved from the Scopus database on February 17, 2025 using a comprehensive set of search terms related to AI and CE, yielding 6, 057 records. After applying Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-based screening criteria covering publication period (2001–2024), subject areas (computer science, business, management, accounting, decision sciences, social sciences and psychology), document type (journal articles), publication stage (final) and language (English) and eliminating duplicates, 1, 241 studies were retained. Bibliometric analysis was conducted using MS Excel, VOSviewer and Biblioshiny (R Studio) to examine publication trends, leading contributors, journals, affiliations and countries. Network mapping through citation, bibliographic coupling and keyword analysis identified intellectual structures. From these, 88 interconnected articles formed the core data set for thematic synthesis, which was carried out using the theory–context–characteristics–methodology (TCCM)-based framework. Findings – AI–CE research has expanded from three publications in 2001 to 690 in 2024. Lee emerged as the most prolific author (15 papers), while Li was the most influential (410 citations). IEEE Access, Expert Systems with Applications, Sustainability, and Computers in Human Behavior were top outlets. Leading institutions included Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Griffith University and Northeastern University, with strong USA–China collaborations. Science mapping identified five clusters: (1) AI and digital transformation (business model innovation and value cocreation), (2) AI–human interaction (interface design and transparency), (3) AI-powered service agents (chatbots, trust and brand outcomes), (4) AI service quality (human–AI complementarity and retention) and (5) AI and privacy (trust and ethical concerns). The TCCM synthesis revealed gaps in theory (limited sociopsychological/value-based models), context (dominance of developed economies and select sectors), characteristics (privacy, ethics and algorithmic bias underexplored) and methods (reliance on cross-sectional surveys). The three-layer framework shows that CE acts as both a direct and indirect pathway linking AI determinants to purchase outcomes. Originality/value – This paper presents a substantive conceptual advancement by offering a comprehensive and integrative synthesis of research in this field. It integrates the bibliometric analysis with the unified three-layer framework from foundational knowledge (TCCM) to conceptual pathways mapping AI–CE to purchase intention linking AI determinants, CE and purchase behavior, while systematically identifying theoretical, contextual, characteristic and methodological gaps. This integration links theoretical and empirical insights, transforming TCCM into a decision-oriented tool with sector-specific managerial implications and societal/policy implications. The value of this study lies in guiding future research by highlighting underexplored theories, diverse contexts, ethical and privacy considerations and advanced research design. © 2026 Emerald Publishing Limited

Title: Decision gatekeepers: how hedonic vs. utilitarian products shape differential persuasion effects in LLM-mediated recommendations
Authors: Pescher A.
Abstract: As consumers increasingly rely on AI for purchase guidance, large language models (LLMs) have become key mediators of buying decisions, processing marketing content before generating recommendations. Understanding how these AI-based decision support systems respond to persuasive techniques becomes critical for consumers and system designers. This study maps LLM response patterns to persuasive techniques across product types. Using a controlled experiment with 13,500 observations across three LLMs (GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Mini, Kimi K2-0905), the research tested hedonic versus utilitarian products under four persuasion conditions based on Cialdini’s principles. Results reveal differential persuasion sensitivity by product type: social proof increased the rate at which LLMs expressed high recommendation certainty for concert tickets from 9.6% to 65.6%, while authority appeals reduced certainty for utilitarian products. This asymmetric pattern persisted across all models and partially mirrors human consumer psychology, suggesting LLMs internalized decision frameworks from training data. The study contributes to IS research by extending the hedonic-utilitarian framework to AI-mediated decision support and connecting LLM persuasion susceptibility to debates on technology trust. These findings have practical implications for how persuasive content shapes AI-mediated consumer decision support. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: An Agent-Based Simulation Model Integrating Generative AI and Fast and Frugal Heuristics for Enhanced Marketing Automation
Authors: Remondino M.; Gaudiello A.
Abstract: This paper introduces an agent-based simulation model integrating generative AI with fast and frugal heuristics to enhance marketing automation. The model adopts fast and frugal heuristics as the primary decision mechanism, invoking generative AI only when situations are ambiguous or exceed the scope of rule-based evaluation. Unlike traditional black-box systems, the architecture preserves interpretability by structuring decisions through transparent heuristic gates before any AI-based reasoning. Central to the framework is a Multi-Agent System (MAS) that simulates customer behaviors and marketing strategies through specialized agents. By leveraging a Vector Database (VecDB) of historical data, the model enables effective personalization without customer-specific fine-tuning. The framework, designed as both a research and a strategic decision-support tool, addresses current limitations in automation by adapting to real-time market dynamics while ensuring transparency through an Explainability Insights Agent. Simulation results demonstrate significant improvements in customer engagement and retention, providing a pathway for interpretable AI-human collaboration in marketing. © 2026, Societa Editrice Il Mulino. Title: From personalization to novelty: AI's role in elevating e-commerce experience
Authors: Anggraeni A.; Hutagaol-Martowidjojo Y.; Meivitawanli B.; Silalahi A.T.; Tohang V.; Talaue F.
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) assists e-commerce users in making transaction decisions through voice, image search, and recommendation features thereby improving shopping efficiency. AI has transformed consumer experience as individuals increasingly rely on it for purchase decisions, resulting in a more personalized shopping experience. However, despite the growing focus on AI and its diverse applications, there has been limited research examining the factors that influence sustained intention to use AI in the e-commerce sector. This study aims to understand the unified online customer experience and identify the many touchpoints through which consumers engage with brands. This study contributes to existing literature by exploring different aspects of AI usage in the e-commerce context while also highlighting the evolving landscape of AI applications in marketing. This research uses quantitative methodology by collecting primary data through the distribution of online questionnaires. The questions measure customer satisfaction, human laziness, novelty seeking, and the intention to continue using AI. The study reveals that e-commerce companies should cater to customers’ novelty-seeking traits by providing new experiences while shopping on e-commerce platforms. In addition, the study demonstrates that enhancing customers’ AI service experience is crucial to sustaining their intention to utilize AI. © 2026 Anggraeni, Hutagaol-Martowidjojo, Meivitawanli, Silalahi, Tohang and Talaue.

Title: Technological and geopolitical disruptions shaping processes and organization design: implications for purchasing and supply management
Authors: Bals L.; Turkulainen V.; Karalis I.; Geraci D.
Abstract: Purpose – New emerging technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence (AI), and changing geopolitical realities provoke the question of whether operations and supply chain management (OSCM) processes, as well as the way they are organized, need to change. Taking the exemplary context of purchasing and supply management (PSM), what might have traditionally been effective and efficient ways to manage and organize PSM processes might be less so in times of AI utilization and autonomous buying and the current geopolitical situation. Design/methodology/approach – This is a perspectives paper. We take a conceptual approach and build on research on PSM processes, the contingency approach to purchasing and supply organizations (PSOs), information processing theory (IPT), organizational buying behavior (OBB) and complement this with illustrative business examples. Findings – The findings highlight a variety of impacts that technological and geopolitical disruptions have on PSM processes and organization. Technological advances may facilitate increased automation and analytical capability, eliminate biases and facilitate pooling of more information and, in general, higher information processing capacity for decision-making, but they also increase the complexity of managing supply chains. Geopolitical tensions, on the other hand, increase, for example, the need to manage various and changing tariffs and trade policies, increasing both uncertainty and complexity. Moreover, the empirical illustrations highlight that the effects of geopolitical disruptions on organizational structures seem more immediate than the effects of technological disruptions. Research limitations/implications – This perspectives paper seeks to spark future PSM research. Beyond that, the five future research avenues are meant to inspire future research in other functions such as operations, logistics, supply chain management, IT, R&D and marketing. Practical implications – The findings underline the strategic importance of PSM for handling an increasingly complex and uncertain business environment by addressing the why, what and how of such a transformation: First, identifying strategic value and strengthening cross-functional collaboration. Second, identifying top AI use cases and adjusting PSM processes and organization accordingly. Third, investing in (digital) transformation capacity and skills (e.g. COEs) contingent upon initial purchasing maturity. Fundamental process redesigns might be required in light of new technologies and geopolitical disruptions, which would then imply the need for (micro-level) PSO redesign, such as defining new job profiles (specialization), as well as adapted cross-functional collaboration patterns (participation) and standard operating procedures (standardization). Social implications – The ongoing high-pace developments in technologies as well as major changes in geopolitical realities create new challenges for both on-the-job training and higher education. This perspectives paper highlights five areas for research, education, and practice for the exemplary function of PSM to help researchers, educators, students and practitioners cope with these challenges and to develop competences and solutions for the future. Originality/value – This perspectives paper highlights the importance of a conversation on the impact of technological and geopolitical changes for the management of PSM processes and organizational considerations. It moreover highlights the future research opportunities on the potential interaction of technological and geopolitical disruptions. © 2026 Emerald Publishing Limited

Title: Beyond human attention: AI-to-AI communication as the next frontier in marketing
Authors: Mogali N.
Abstract: Traditional marketing has long been designed around capturing and sustaining human attention. As digital saturation reaches new heights and consumer decision making becomes increasingly mediated by technology, this paradigm is undergoing significant transformation.The rise of autonomous agents such as artificial intelligence (AI) systems acting on behalf of consumers, businesses and institutions, signals a fundamental shift in approach. Marketing messages are no longer directed primarily at humans but at algorithms and virtual agents making choices on their behalf. This paper explores AI-to-AI communication as the next frontier in marketing.The paper examines the current state of attention-based models and the technological advancements driving this change. It also highlights the accelerating deployment of consumer and enterprise AI agents across some major industries. Benefits of this shift include hyper-personalisation, streamlined transactions and reduced cognitive burden on human decision makers. Risks include working with algorithmic black boxes, erosion of human trust and the potential concentration of influence among a small set of dominant AI platforms. By framing marketing as an ecosystem where algorithms negotiate, filter and prioritise on behalf of stakeholders, this paper emphasises that organisations must redefine brand strategy for this new reality. Readers can learn about the strategic recommendations for adapting marketing practices in a world where AI agents, not humans, are often the primary audience.This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at http://hstalks.com/business. © HENRY STEWART PUBLICATIONS.

Title: Agentic AI in Branding: Driving Hyper-personalization and Real-time Adaptation
Authors: Puri S.; Pradhan J.A.; Bernabe B.G.; Ray A.K.
Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems capable of independent decision-making, learning and adaptation, is redefining branding by transforming passive consumer interactions into dynamic, co-creative relationships. This article synthesizes contemporary research (2020–2024) to explore how agentic AI enables hyper-personalized experiences, facilitates real-time brand adaptation and addresses ethical challenges in consumer engagement. Through case studies from Coca-Cola, Netflix and Unilever, we illustrate how autonomous AI systems enhance customer loyalty, drive innovation and foster trust through transparency. The study advocates strong governance of agentic AI through clearly defined policies, structured review points, audit documentation and escalation protocols to manage risks such as algorithmic bias and brand inconsistency. It offers managers a practical framework for implementation: establish brand guidelines, incorporate human oversight at critical decision points and monitor outcomes to ensure AI enhances rather than replaces human judgement. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for collaboration among marketing, data science, design and ethics teams to align AI autonomy with long-term brand integrity. It also highlights future research opportunities in areas such as crisis management protocols, AI-to-AI customer interactions and cultural adaptability in automated systems. © 2026 IMI

Title: Familiarity with a brand makes customers more sensitive to AI-generated marketing content: insights from Destination Marketing and Framing Theory
Authors: Holopainen J.; Tuominen S.; Konttinen N.; Pesonen J.
Abstract: Existing literature has highlighted the lower performance of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated marketing content in conveying affective messaging. Affective messaging is especially important in tourism and destination marketing. While recent literature highlights increasing human involvement in content creation potential solution, we argue that this approach aligns with framing theory, as both seek to enhance content presentation to effectively influence consumer information processing and decision-making. Framing theory emphasises consumers’ subject familiarity as a critical factor; however, this dimension has not been considered a boundary condition in current research on AI-driven marketing content creation. Using an online quasi-experiment with one destination marketing brand, we compared three content sources: human-created content, AI-generated content, and AI-generated content with increased human involvement. Based on a sample of university staff and students, the results show that audiences with low brand familiarity were less sensitive to AI-generated marketing content than familiar audiences. Meanwhile, increasing human involvement in content creation diminished negative attitudes toward AI use. These results highlight consumers’ subject familiarity as a significant factor affecting perceptions of AI-generated marketing content. The findings contribute to the existing literature on factors shaping perceptions of AI-generated marketing content, while also advancing framing theory and research on human involvement in marketing communications. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Determinants of customer acceptance in AI-powered conversational agents: A systematic literature review and research agenda
Authors: Deilen M.; De-Juan-Vigaray M.D.; Runia P.; Parra Meroño M.C.
Abstract: As conversational AI agents (CAIAs) become embedded in customer–firm interactions, the theoretical models employed to account for their acceptance increasingly appear inappropriate. This systematic literature review synthesizes 58 empirical studies (2018–2025) and exposes a core tension: established frameworks such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) rest on assumptions of instrumentally rational users evaluating stable system attributes, yet CAIAs are adaptive, probabilistic, and socially responsive in ways that render those assumptions problematic. The resulting mismatch, we argue, is responsible for contradictory empirical findings, particularly at the intersection of trust, anthropomorphism, and perceived risk. Where rationalist models fall short, the Computers as Social Actors (CASA) paradigm proves more apt at capturing relational dynamics, though it too offers only a partial account. By distinguishing between utilitarian and relational agent types and between high-stakes and low-stakes decision contexts, the review uncovers boundary conditions that earlier syntheses have left unexamined. Drawing on consumer decision-making, value co-creation, and relationship management scholarship, we develop a marketing-centred research agenda comprising five theoretically grounded directions. Managerial guidance is offered for CAIA design attuned to distinct phases of the customer journey. © 2026 Korean Scholars of Marketing Science.
